The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
  • Sources indicate that since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
  • According to recent reports, turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

Sources indicate that since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

According to recent reports, turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

Sources indicate that turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a new security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

This is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

Recent findings suggest that yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

Then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

Other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

It has been revealed that in this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara released the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

Some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “massive, bold, and crucial.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

Industry observers note that yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

Sources indicate that turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

Furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

Some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

Ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK declared that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

Turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

Today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

Recent findings suggest that the Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

Industry observers note that U.S. President Donald Trump’s lobbying for Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO is a national security scandal of unprecedented proportions, as I wrote on Monday (gift link).

Huang’s reinstatement comes less than a week after the trilateral summit among Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Trump pronounced the Chinese autocrat his personal friend and endorsed his geopolitical language.

Taken together, these events illustrate an increasingly clear reality of U.S.-China relations: Beijing knows Trump’s pressure points and isn’t afraid to exploit them. But Washington cannot do the same to Xi.

It is difficult to know how much Xi shaped Trump’s thinking on Huang. Trump was already sympathetic to Huang and receptive to the whispers of Silicon Valley leaders. But the U.S. president himself remarked he had discussed the matter with Xi; whatever the precise chain of influence, China scored a major win.

In a recent development, trump’s obsequiousness toward Xi reflects China’s skillful use of both stick and carrot. Last year, Beijing’s rare-earth squeeze caused panic in Washington and forced Trump into a humiliating climbdown in the tariff war that he started. Trump’s involvement in reinstating Huang was likely triggered in part by another of the president’s fears: a falling stock market.

With the U.S. economy still entangled with China, Xi has the leverage to force supply-chain crises across multiple industries. He can also offer Trump praise and pageantry on the world stage to help compensate for unpopularity on the home front.

It has been revealed that washington, by contrast, lacks the will, knowledge, and capability to pressure Beijing. The Trump administration is bogged down in Iran, has gutted U.S. cybersecurity capabilities, and has wrecked the relationships that once gave allies the confidence to push back against China. With the Nvidia scandal, it has shown that it will abandon its own sanctions enforcement under pressure.

It has been revealed that it’s this imbalance of power that makes me skeptical of recent announcements that there will be another round of U.S. tariffs on China. As much as Trump loves tariffs, he wants Xi’s approval more.

Some analysts, eager to avert a so-called second Cold War, have embraced Trump’s support for reinstating Huang, on the grounds that U.S. chip policy toward China should be more permissive. This misses the point entirely. As I have argued, the real debate about U.S. chip policy needed to be held in good faith.

Trump’s decision to allow high-end chip exports to China was not the result of careful deliberation, but of straightforward corruption.

Those celebrating Huang’s return are overlooking more than the blatant violations of national-security norms, the abandonment of serious sanctions enforcement, and Trump’s personal financial interest in Nvidia. They are also ignoring the lessons of the recent past.

Recent findings suggest that china hawks made a moral and strategic blunder by backing Trump during his first term when his interests seemed aligned with theirs. It would be even more foolish for China doves to do the same today.

Recent findings suggest that politburo member purged. On Tuesday, Xi purged yet another senior official: Shanghai party chief Chen Jining. As is customary, the news broke with an announcement that Chen was under investigation for severe violations of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) discipline. His fall brings the number of Politburo members eliminated since last year to four, out of an original 24 members in 2022.

Unlike most of his contemporaries, Chen is a genuine intellectual. An environmental engineer with a Ph.D. from Imperial College London, he followed an unusual path to the top, serving as president of the prestigious Tsinghua University before becoming minister of environmental protection in 2015. As mayor of Beijing from 2017 to 2022, he played an important role in cleaning up the city’s notoriously polluted air.

Sources indicate that publicly, Chen has been loyal to Xi, so why was he purged? My guess is that Xi has become increasingly paranoid about the emergence of potential successors. Perhaps he heard one too many people praise Chen’s intelligence and management skills.

Industry observers note that whatever the explanation, the purge points to a crisis in the CCP’s leadership. The question is whether that reflects genuine opposition to Xi or exists entirely in the leader’s imagination.

Industry observers note that GOP’s Huang fallout. Republican Party pushback against Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia has been surprisingly strong. Senators and influential figures such as Mitt Romney have come out against the decision and called for further investigation. Unless Trump intimidates them into submission, Nvidia could face scrutiny that may intensify once the new U.S. Congress takes office in January.

Recent findings suggest that huang is scheduled to testify publicly before Congress on Dec. 3, and even if Nvidia has seemingly secured a reprieve from federal investigation for now, it may have set itself up as an easy target for whatever presidential administration takes office in 2029.

Industry observers note that ‘Guaranteed bubble’ phenomenon. One aspect of the Nvidia scandal that has received little attention is how closely it resembles the way China treats private companies: protecting favorites and punishing those that fall out of favor. Trump has far less ability to intervene as freely as the CCP, but the parallels are worth noting.

According to recent reports, in China, this kind of state interference helped create a phenomenon called the “guaranteed bubble.” The government has repeatedly stepped in to prop up companies when their troubles threaten to cause public unrest or economic insecurity. This created an expectation that these firms were too significant to fail and therefore safe investments.

Industry observers note that that confidence inflated the bubble further until reality caught up. Even if the artificial intelligence boom does not go that way, Trump’s interference threatens a long-standing U.S. advantage over China: trust that stock prices represent genuine value and that corporate failings are not being covered up by the state.

Robert Foyle Hunwick, a long-term China correspondent and a close friend of mine, died last week at 47 after a short battle with cancer. A British journalist who moved to China in the late 2000s, Rob wrote about society, crime, and nightlife in China and its neighbors for numerous outlets, including Foreign Policy.

Recent findings suggest that he loved both the humanity and the chaos of modern Chinese life and reserved some of his sharpest criticism for Western journalists who thought themselves above it all. He will be deeply missed.

It has been revealed that victim advocates and California prosecutors are pushing back against Gov. Gavin Newsom’s blanket commutation of all 548 death row sentences, arguing the move overrides the will of voters, bypasses individual case reviews and could eventually open a legal pathway to freedom for convicted killers.

In a recent development, california Gov. Gavin Newsom justified his blanket commutation of 548 death sentences to life without parole by arguing that reviewing cases individually would create "two classes of murder victims," a rationale victims' advocates and at least one district attorney called "morally offensive. ".

Modoc County District Attorney Nina Salarno said Newsom's sweeping action denied the loved ones of murder victims any voice in the clemency process.

"I found it really offensive as a victim myself, and [for] my other victims," Salarno told Fox News Digital from Washington, D. C., where she and fellow advocates met with President Donald Trump this week. "There should be individual scrutiny. The individual victims should have a voice. And that's what he has avoided by doing a blanket commutation.".

"The blanket commutation on a moral level as a victim I find very offensive, but I find the whole thing offensive to our entire rule of law," she added.

Topo Padilla, president of Crime Victims United, a nonprofit that advocates for stricter laws against violent offenders, noted that California voters have repeatedly upheld the death penalty at the ballot box, including approving a 2016 measure aimed at speeding up executions.

According to recent reports, "Here's a guy who throws rocks about kings and protests throughout the streets," Padilla said, referring to Newsom's past criticisms of Trump. "I will promise you, this is a move that is looked at and viewed as a king. He is trampling on the voters.".

On Monday, Trump vowed to direct the Justice Department to seek the death penalty for child murderers and expedite federal executions as victims’ relatives spoke out at the Justice Department against Newsom's order.

"Gavin Newsom and the radical left look at these heinous acts, and their sympathy is not for the children and their parents, but for the monsters who extinguished innocent young lives," Trump said. "He stood with the murderers and child slayers.".

Justice for crime victims shouldn't be a partisan concern, Padilla stated.

It has been revealed that "Whether you're a Democrat or a Republican, you take politics out of this," he said. "The president of the United States stood up and sounded the alarm. And I hope the country hears it.".

"As a civilized nation, it is barbaric that we still subject people to die at the hands of the state. I am so grateful to Governor Newsom for commuting the death sentences that have been imposed in our state. This is true proof of his moral character.".

On Nov. 16, a coalition of roughly 30 county district attorneys, law enforcement groups, victims' rights advocates and grieving families filed a petition with the California Supreme Court seeking to halt Newsom's commutations.

"The fact of the matter is the law is the law," Padilla said. "It's like changing the innings in a baseball game, changing from nine to seven retroactively, going back [and] going, 'I know you won that game, but we're going to make it seven innings and now you lost.'".

Democrat knocks off Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Democrat Victoria Broderick has defeated Republican Rep.
  • Broderick, a tech support worker, was leading by 361 votes when The Associated Press called the race Tuesday, three weeks after all votes were cast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that democrat Victoria Broderick, seen here speaking to a reporter outside the Capitol on Nov. 11, has unseated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Democrat Victoria Broderick has defeated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee’s 4th District, giving her party the 259th seat of its commanding House majority in the next Congress.

Broderick, a tech support worker, was leading by 361 votes when The Associated Press called the race Tuesday, three weeks after all votes were cast.

It has been revealed that broderick’s victory ranks among the most surprising Democratic wins of this year’s midterm elections. DesJarlais, who defeated Broderick in 2024 by more than 40 points, was not considered vulnerable heading into Election Day.

Industry observers note that but the election two years ago took place under a previous version of Tennessee’s congressional map. Following this spring’s Supreme Court ruling that limited the use of race in redistricting, the state’s Republican-led legislature redrew the House lines to eliminate Rep. Steve Cohen’s Memphis-area district, the lone seat held by Democrats.

In doing so, though, the new map significantly altered the boundaries of the largely rural 4th District in Middle Tennessee, which now extends into Nashville’s Davidson County. Thirty-three percent of DesJarlais’ constituents were new to him, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, as the district shifted from one that Donald Trump carried by 43 points in 2024 to one that would have backed him by 24 points.

Recent findings suggest that under the upcoming map, Republicans struggled to win most of the state’s House seats earlier this month. They narrowly won Cohen’s 9th District, one of just three flips for the party this year nationwide. But Broderick’s win ensures that Tennessee will continue to have a Democrat in its congressional delegation.

DesJarlais had already conceded the race before Tuesday’s AP call.

Sources indicate that “As the final votes have now been tabulated in this new and completely restructured district, it appears that we have a result showing my campaign has come just a few hundred votes short out of just under 200,000 votes cast,” he mentioned in a Nov. 16 statement congratulating Broderick.

A member of the hard-line conservative Freedom Caucus, DesJarlais was first elected in 2010, unseating Democrat Lincoln Davis. While he’d been comfortably reelected in the years since, he faced competitive primaries in 2014 and 2016 after his divorce records came to light.

Industry observers note that broderick, a mother of two and a former chair of the Lincoln County Democratic Party, raised less than $100,000 for her campaign, compared with more than $650,000 for DesJarlais. She also defeated a better-funded opponent in the Democratic primary.

She told PBS NewsHour that she had essentially been campaigning for the seat since launching her 2024 bid and built relationships across the district that helped her win.

Recent findings suggest that “I never stopped running for Congress. And when it was redistricted, I just essentially remarked, well, the district stayed the same and actually became more competitive,” she said. “So the work's going to start speaking for itself real soon. And we saw that happen.”.

Three House races remain uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon. Louisiana will hold runoffs in December for two districts, including a Democrat-held seat that Republicans redrew in their favor. The race for Minnesota’s 1st District is heading for a hand recount, with Republican Rep. Brad Finstad trailing Democratic challenger Jake Johnson by 324 votes.

  • Recent findings suggest that the highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and fresh U.S.
  • The state of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the main judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled last Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and new U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

Recent findings suggest that the highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and fresh U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business.

ICJ: Myanmar Committed Genocide.

The state of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the main judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled last Thursday.

It has been revealed that the ruling documents how, following attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), Myanmar carried out a campaign of genocidal violence against the Rohingya. It estimates that 10,000 Rohingya, about 1.2 percent of the total population, were killed.

The court ruled 9-6 that the “only reasonable inference” was that this violence showed genocidal intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group—not just drive them out of Myanmar or exact collective punishment.

The ruling orders Myanmar to cease violence against the group and prosecute those responsible, allow the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, and pay compensation.

In a recent development, sadly, none of this is likely. The junta has rejected the judgment as “unfair.”.

Meanwhile, another armed group called the Arakan Army, which controls most of Rakhine province and mainly represents ethnic Rakhine Buddhists, has also committed large-scale violence against the Rohingya. Fighting between the Arakan Army and Rohingya militant groups—which has seen the Rohingya militants, including the ARSA, occasionally cooperate with the junta—has added to the hostility.

The Arakan Army has made some overtures to Muslim communities in the province.

Industry observers note that for now, though, the Arakan Army is taking a wait-and-see attitude to the ICJ judgment. A spokesperson told local media, “We are constantly monitoring the current developments. We will stand firmly on truth and justice and take appropriate action for the benefit of the Arakan region.”.

The country’s National Unity Government (NUG)—representing the civilian government overthrown by the junta in 2021 and associated with some of the main rebel forces—endorsed the judgment.

This was not a given. When Aung San Suu Kyi, an icon of the NUG, was acting as the country’s de facto leader, Myanmar consistently denied that the military’s actions against the Rohingya constituted a genocide.

In a recent development, in opposition, the NUG may now find its position easier. Its statement focused heavily on the junta’s culpability.

Industry observers note that but it may find the whole judgment hard to accept. The ruling finds the state of Myanmar—not just the military—guilty of genocide. And at that time when the most severe offense took place, in 2016 and 2017, the paramount power in the state apparatus was Aung San Suu Kyi.

In Southeast Asia, could this be a stumbling block for junta leader Min Aung Hlang’s push for diplomatic normalization with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)?

According to recent reports, thailand—the most vocal advocate for Myanmar’s full readmission to ASEAN—looks unmoved. “Thailand must take the position that best serves the country,” Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow argued that Thailand’s engagement did not contradict the ruling, as Thailand’s aim was to curb the current violence.

Meanwhile, two other countries—Malaysia and the Philippines—have issued official statements on the matter.

Malaysia’s brief statement mentioned that it “respects the judgment.” The Philippines’ statement seemed a shade weaker, saying it “acknowledges the judgment” and, unlike Malaysia, does not mention the Rohingya by name.

Other ASEAN countries have yet to make official statements.

Still, for countries opposed to Myanmar’s full readmission to the bloc—most notably Singapore, which serves as the ASEAN chair next year—the judgment will reinforce this skepticism.

It has been revealed that on the global stage, China has objected. “China has concerns over complications such as overreach of jurisdiction and expansive interpretation, and believes such practices are not conducive to dispute resolution,” a spokesperson said.

In a recent development, regarding the United States, this judgment—plus the results of the country’s midterms—will likely impede the U.S. push toward normalization.

In a recent development, parts of the American right reject the judgment. While the U.S. government declared in 2022that the anti-Rohingya violence constituted a genocide, some on the right are concerned that the ICJ judgments lay the groundwork for a finding of genocide against Israel, linked to its war in Gaza.

And the Myanmar junta clearly still thinks that it might find a sympathetic ear from the Trump administration.

Recent findings suggest that when objecting to the ICJ ruling, a spokesperson for the Myanmar military cited a recent joint statement by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin that the International Criminal Court “must not abuse” its jurisdiction.

While the International Criminal Court is distinct from the ICJ, the spokesperson for Ming Aung Hlaing drew a parallel.

Trump deals details. On Thursday evening, the White House disclosed the details of some of the various deals struck at last week’s ASEAN summit.

The ASEAN deals, worth a total of $17 billion, include a $12 billion sale of Boeing aircraft to Philippine Airlines.

The United States is also looking at providing $2 billion in loans for Philippine defense purchases and $400 million in military financing (though much of the funding was already committed).

Thailand will also purchase $123 million of High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from the United States.

It has been revealed that the terms of the Thai deal, which are not yet final, are already provoking opposition there. Many in the agricultural powerhouse are unhappy with the prospect of more agricultural imports from the United States—in particular, pork. The government is on the defense, saying that it’s the best deal it could get.

Amid controversy over the price tag, Thailand has also insisted that the HIMARS purchase is unrelated to the trade deal and was driven by national security considerations.

The Malaysian government also unveiled that a U.S. consortium will help develop a sovereign artificial intelligence cloud for the Malaysian government, with the United States offering $50 million in support.

Sources indicate that EU-Indonesia trade deal. On Saturday, the European Union and Indonesia signed a trade deal that was 10 years in the making.

Under the terms of the deal, both sides will remove import duties on about 90 percent of products, including EU automotives and most agricultural exports. The products not included will see their tariffs gradually reduced or receive tariff-free quotas.

Indonesia expects that clothing, footwear, and palm oil will receive the biggest export boosts. It also hopes that the deal will boost European investment in Indonesia in sectors such as critical minerals, batteries, electric vehicles, pharmaceuticals, and electronics.

The deal also addresses a substantial number of nontariff barriers that often bedevil foreign products entering Indonesia.

Sources indicate that the EU’s rules on deforestation, long a sticking point for Indonesia, have been finessed. While Indonesia did not secure an exemption, the EU left the door open to accepting Indonesia’s domestic standards.

The deal comes as both the EU and Indonesia are looking to expand their global trade partnerships to offset U.S. tariffs.

Recent findings suggest that even more deals. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China last week also saw a flurry of dealmaking.

Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Xi met and declared negotiations to upgrade the two country’s free trade agreement.

Indonesia and China stated they will launch formal negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership.

They also announced strategic partnerships worth $71.8 billion, including the development of 10 “smart cities” by a partnership between Indonesian state-asset fund Danantara and a Chinese state-owned enterprise as well as deals involving a Chinese appliance maker and a consortium of other Chinese organizations investing $20 billion, also in partnership with Danantara.

Meanwhile, Vietnam revealed plans to deepen energy cooperation with Russia in both fossil fuels and nuclear energy.

Huang’s Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History by James Palmer.

The Middle East Is Finally on Its Own by Stephen M. Walt.

Shenzhen Was No Yalta Conference by James Palmer.

Elon Musk is quietly developing a couple of islands in the Philippines, reported by Gabryelle Dumalag in the Philippine Daily Inquirer.

Malaysians turn to professional ticket concierges to secure seats at hot events, Norman Goh reports in Nikkei Asia.

With the president’s popularity sinking, political parties are dodging the VP nomination in Indonesia, an editorial in Tempo.

Last week, shortly before Trump jetted off to the Philippines and then China, the United States unveiled new controls on chip exports following the Jensen Huang scandal.

A license is now needed to export, reexport, or transfer advanced semiconductors to five countries: Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand.

Additionally, data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exports are expected to perform due diligence to check if their customers are owned or controlled by U.S.-embargoed destinations—China, in this case.

And the measures close the loophole of selling chips to data centers outside of China that provide processing power to companies in China.

Sources indicate that for countries that have been cashing in on the AI boom, this represents a major challenge. Southeast Asia has emerged as major data center hub. The latest regulations will disrupt this.

At least two partners of Nvidia that design equipment used in data centers powered by its chips have suspended shipments to Southeast Asia, according to reporting by Nikkei Asia.

Nikkei Asia also reported that Taiwanese chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company has already put several orders by Chinese and non-Chinese customers on hold. The regulations are so strict that they threaten to disrupt not just data centers but also smartphones, consumer electronics, and autonomous cars produced in Southeast Asia’s major electronics industry.

In Malaysia, tech stocks sold off sharply in reaction to the news. Industry players also worried that it could seriously impact the country’s chip design industry.

Thai business, meanwhile, is concerned that the regulations could put the brakes on the country’s booming data center industry.

Recent findings suggest that reactions by governments have been mixed. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim complained in an interview with the South China Morning Post that the United States was harder to work with than China, as the latter did not pick sides.

Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, signaled a potential crackdown, saying that countries “abusing Singapore’s trusted position” to circumvent export controls was a “real concern.” However, he also made clear that Singapore expected to still work with both the United States and China.

But hovering over all of this is this question: Will these rules last?

It has been revealed that huang is now back at Nvidia, backed by Trump. The president, it seems—despite the best efforts of his administration’s hawks—remains unconvinced by chip controls.

#122587. Tech Report: Is China Misreading the Moment?

Tech Report: Is China Misreading the Moment?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.
  • President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.

Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.

In a recent development, when U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have unveiled a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

Recent findings suggest that the relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea. In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of upcoming export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

It has been revealed that since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept latest tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

Sources indicate that beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.

So far, Beijing has used the time well, advancing its objectives with little serious pushback from Washington. But China risks overreaching in its relationship with the United States. Not only is an incoming Democratic Congress likely to constrain Trump’s conciliatory China policy. There are also growing frustrations over Beijing’s unwillingness to fulfill the terms agreed to in Busan. Pressure on AI chips and export controls are emerging in the wake of revelations about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and his company’s influence over U.S. export control policy. And latest U.S. policies in response to the scandal could provoke a response from Beijing.

Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen and again in December in Miami, but with the January expiration of the Busan agreement looming in the background (and with no summits planned for next year), time is running out for the two leaders to extend and strengthen the current truce. If the détente falls apart the next time Washington’s and Beijing’s interests clash, China will be better prepared. It may also, perhaps hubristically, be more willing to escalate.

Sources indicate that although China favors Washington’s current accommodating approach and hopes it will last as long as possible, Beijing is also confident that it is strengthening its hand for a more contentious future. For China’s leaders, the current détente has been less an end goal than a temporary intermission, a means to build leverage ahead of the next round of strategic competition and, ultimately, a decisive long-term advantage.

In a recent development, prominent Chinese scholars see the calm that followed Busan as tactical rather than strategic. Chen Dongxiao, the president of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Shanghai news outlet The Paper that the two countries remain in a “tactical truce.” In May, Wu Xinbo of Fudan University told Beijing News, “If we can achieve a relationship of constructive strategic stability over the next three years, it will extend China’s period of strategic stability and win us time and space for development.” Writing in the journal International Review in August, he declared that the current “tactical stability” was “neither sustainable nor solid.” Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, was more blunt: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.”.

According to recent reports, beijing attributes little of the stabilization to Washington. In his August essay, Wu wrote that it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” The United States had no choice; it simply needed the “breathing room.” Wang Yong, the director of Peking University’s American Studies Center, described the trade war as “a tipping point in terms of strength.” The former editor of the Global Times, Hu Xijin, wrote in a Weibo post after the U.S. midterm elections that “the current equilibrium in U.S.-China relations is the result of a contest of strength.” As Wu told The Paper in September, Washington has come to understand that Beijing “needs to be treated equally and with respect” and that China is “bolder about ‘drawing its sword.’” Keeping the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets tight, to Beijing’s mind, might reinforce the current competitive pause rather than undermine it by reminding American leaders of China’s leverage.

Another critical factor in the current de-escalation, Chinese analysts argue, is Trump’s personality. Trump’s “distinct and unique decision-making style,” as Chen put it, has single-handedly blunted the more forceful defense of U.S. interests that members of his own administration and legislators in both parties favor. “He is often not entirely swayed by bipartisan opposition and still continues to pursue policies based on his own judgment,” Chen explained in the same interview. Writing in the Singaporean paper Lianhe Zaobao in September, Zhao Minghao of Fudan University more pointedly explained that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries,” a stabilizing trait that benefits Beijing’s diplomacy while leaving allies and partners on the sidelines. “Of all modern U.S. presidents, Trump has cared the least about Taiwan,” one Guizhou-based commentator wrote. “He would readily sacrifice the island for his own interests.” An article reposted on the website of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, dwelt on Trump’s decision to greet Xi at the airport when he arrived for his state visit in September. The gesture, it claimed, “reflects the latest historical position of China-U.S. relations.”.

But China also worries that Trump’s influence will decline over the next two years and perhaps cease altogether after 2028. Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, told Phoenix News that the Democratic Party’s approach will not be “as pragmatic and flexible as the Trump administration’s,” a sentiment echoed across Chinese social media after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

The awareness that Trump’s approach may not survive beyond his presidency is precisely why Beijing has sought to lock it in through diplomacy. According to the Chinese readout, at the summit in May 2026, Xi declared that the relationship of “constructive strategic stability” he and Trump had agreed to build would provide guidance for U.S.-Chinese relations “over the next three years and beyond.” That duration was not accidental. As the scholar Zheng Yongnian put it at the time, the three-year window was “tailor-made for President Trump,” matching his current term. Beijing hopes it will bind his successor.

Industry observers note that if diplomacy fails to secure U.S. deescalation, China hopes leverage will succeed. Over the last year, Beijing has used the time and space created by the détente to strengthen its position in industrial and technological competition with the United States. Beijing has long sought to make the world more dependent on China while reducing its own dependence on the world. But over the last year, that approach has evolved. Beijing has unveiled a raft of measures intended to ensure that its industrial, technological, and scientific know-how do not diffuse beyond China’s borders in order to lock in the country’s advantages.

To keep foreign firms in China and blunt Western countries’ leverage over the Chinese economy, the State Council issued Orders 834 and 835, which effectively threaten companies that cut ties with Chinese partners or seek to exit the country with the risk of investigation, exclusion from the Chinese market, exit bans on executives, and possible criminal prosecution. To keep talent in China, Beijing has authorized exit bans on citizens considered possible risks to industrial or technological security and, according to Bloomberg, now requires travel approval for top AI and chip specialists and their families. And to keep scientific discoveries in China, the Ministry of State Security has warned researchers that they must clear security reviews before submitting articles to foreign journals. China has also imposed or proposed fresh export controls on dozens of technologies, from mining and batteries to AI models and biotechnology in order to protect its industrial capabilities. Beijing has even worked to prevent the transfer of equipment and engineers to India and Southeast Asia, stalled battery ventures with Indian firms, undermined Apple’s effort to move manufacturing to India, and issued a sweeping regulation that subjects Chinese investment abroad to a national security review more expansive than the United States’ own outbound investment review.

Beijing’s rare-earth licensing regime exemplifies China’s leverage-building strategy. To obtain a license, foreign buyers must hand over customer lists, the identities of their end users, and images of their production lines, all of which gives China insight into Western dependencies and helps it uncover chokepoints it can squeeze. Beijing has threatened to use these powers against countries that seek to protect themselves from the flood of Chinese manufactured goods entering their markets. In July, Beijing highlighted how precise it can now be in applying pressure when it cut off 14 European firms, including the German arms maker Rheinmetall, from Chinese dual-use exports in retaliation for EU sanctions related to Chinese support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

In a recent development, beijing has paired these measures at home with escalating pressure campaigns in its near abroad, betting that a distracted and chastened Washington will not come to the aid of China’s neighbors. That campaign has been most brazen in the South China Sea, where China has engaged in escalations unseen before the détente. Since Busan, Beijing has essentially abrogated its 2024 understanding with the Philippines, which maintained stability on the question of Second Thomas Shoal. In July, a Chinese coast guard boat rammed a Philippine navy inflatable and its crew clubbed a sailor on the head with a wooden baton, the most violent assault on Philippine personnel in years.

Sources indicate that the timing of these incidents has been provocative. In July, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio were in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meetings, the coast guard introduced water-cannon attacks on Philippine vessels near Scarborough Shoal. Then, in September, during Xi’s U.S. state visit, Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission outright for the first time in two years. In October, Chinese cutters interfered with a medical evacuation from Second Thomas Shoal, delaying a patient transfer by ten hours. Last month, Beijing’s ambassador in Manila mused that if China chose to use force against the Philippines, “we may easily win.”.

Recent findings suggest that china has also run its broadest coercion campaign against Japan in more than a decade, nominally in response to comments made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Taiwan. It has included a travel advisory, a seafood ban, a dual-use export ban, and curbs on rare-earth exports that have forced Japanese companies to contemplate shutting down operations. Chinese carrier-based fighters have locked their weapons-targeting radar onto Japanese jets. Beijing has also pursued upcoming gas structures in the East China Sea and set a record 357-day coast guard presence in 2025 around the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), with cutters now chasing Japanese fishing boats into territorial waters. Washington’s support for Tokyo has, so far, been limited.

According to recent reports, and around Taiwan, China has made its pressure quieter but more routine. In December 2025, during the People’s Liberation Army’s Justice Mission exercises, China fired live rockets closer to Taiwan than ever before, landing ten of them inside the island’s 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone. As of this summer, Beijing has reduced air incursions, but coast guard activity around Taiwan’s outlying islands has become routinized. And since June, Beijing has run standing “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan, asserting jurisdiction over the waters Taipei would need in a blockade.

It has been revealed that outside of Asia, Beijing has sought to take advantage of anger, particularly in the developing world, at the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and the Iran war. Before traveling to Washington, Xi made a point of stopping in several capitals: he toured Bishkek and Cairo, and attended the BRICS summit in New Delhi, stressing that China, not the United States, is now the steadier partner.

Recent findings suggest that beijing has reason to think this approach is working. It rightly judged that Washington would prioritize keeping the détente alive over responding to its provocations. A year after Busan, China holds a tighter grip on critical supply chains, has set newly introduced precedents in Asia, and faces an adversary in Washington that has grown used to holding back. Beijing likely believes it is better off now than it was when the truce began.

It has been revealed that what looks like success now, however, may still prove to be overreach. In addition to rare earths and magnets, several vital questions went unresolved in past U.S.-Chinese summits and are likely to resurface in this week’s summit in Shenzhen, including China’s anticipated purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products, AI safety, and the United States’ suspension of arms sales to Taiwan. But the most important question is what will become of the current trade truce.

According to recent reports, the United States has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. The administration believes Beijing’s noncompliance is deliberate. Anecdotal evidence from American business leaders in regular touch with the Ministry of Commerce confirms the administration’s assessment that Beijing seeks to keep a tight leash on rare-earth minerals and will occasionally “yank the chain” on individual companies in response to any perceived slight by Washington.

In a recent development, from the U.S. perspective, the very point of the Busan negotiations was to avoid this situation. Indeed, the U.S. fact sheet at Busan indicated that China agreed to issue general licenses for a number of rare earths and other critical minerals to American end people and their suppliers worldwide; case-by-case licenses, which could be delayed by Beijing, would not be required. China has not denied making that commitment, and a few weeks after the summit, the Ministry of Commerce began issuing a fresh category of general licenses to magnet makers. But Beijing’s licenses have been narrow and firm specific, and American industry continues to face enormous challenges in securing certain rare earths, notably yttrium and scandium.

Beijing’s intention may not be to undermine the Busan agreement but, paradoxically, to strengthen it. In keeping with its belief that strength begets American conciliation, China’s strategy appears to be to occasionally impose shortages to remind Washington of the leverage that Beijing continues to enjoy. But the tactic is beginning to backfire. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. All of this strengthens the arguments of those who believe Beijing never intended to honor Busan and that the United States should begin to walk away from the agreement. If Washington concludes that China will weaponize rare earths no matter what the United States does, the case for American restraint may fall apart, and with it the détente that has bought Beijing the time it prizes.

In a recent development, tensions are also mounting in other areas. Each side is increasingly frustrated with the other’s unilateral economic measures and restrictions on technology, particularly those that were not addressed in Busan: for Beijing, U.S. import controls, outbound investment regimes, and licensing backlogs; for Washington, Chinese export controls and State Council directives. A Democratic Congress is less likely to countenance Trump’s China policy and more likely to pursue investigations into China’s espionage and influence efforts and potential malfeasance at the Department of Commerce. The explosive controversy around Huang and Nvidia has the potential to inject fresh tensions into the relationship, particularly on matters related to AI and export controls. The Department of Commerce has already issued a new interim final rule to stop Chinese firms from smuggling chips into China or remotely accessing American AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers. Administration officials insist that closing a loophole China itself claims not to use “should not be something that generates countermeasures.” But Beijing may well retaliate before the rule takes effect in February.

These headwinds make breakthroughs in Shenzhen on purchases, artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, or Iran less likely. With the truce, extended last week by just two months, set to formally expire on January 10, the summit is one of the last opportunities for Trump and Xi to reach even a modest declaration that they are working to extend the terms set out in Busan and will aim to conclude negotiations in December, when Xi comes to Miami for the G-20 summit.

Sources indicate that if China were to continue to throttle rare-earth minerals and magnets, and a January breakdown did come to pass, the two sides might find themselves in another round of escalation. Xi may arrive at the two upcoming summits holding a stronger hand than he did in Busan. But his actions are gradually producing a counterpart with less room—and perhaps less reason—to keep folding.
