In the small eastern German city of Dessau, if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has its way, a century-old vision for the future may soon belong to the past.

It has been revealed that A short walk away from the main train station, past typical German architecture of beige stucco and pitched, red-tiled roofs, flat-roofed, modernist structures of concrete and glass appear, leading to a building with “BAUHAUS” spelled down one gray side. Designed by pioneering modernist architect Walter Gropius, the building in Dessau opened as a school for architecture, craft, and industrial design on Dec. 4, 1926—one with ambitions to create a fresh aesthetic for the modern world. With its steel-framed windows and a bright red entrance door, the Bauhaus school building is an iconic symbol of early 20th-century modernism.

In the small eastern German city of Dessau, if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has its way, a century-old vision for the future may soon belong to the past.

A short walk away from the main train station, past typical German architecture of beige stucco and pitched, red-tiled roofs, flat-roofed, modernist structures of concrete and glass appear, leading to a building with “BAUHAUS” spelled down one gray side. Designed by pioneering modernist architect Walter Gropius, the building in Dessau opened as a school for architecture, craft, and industrial design on Dec. 4, 1926—one with ambitions to create a latest aesthetic for the modern world. With its steel-framed windows and a bright red entrance door, the Bauhaus school building is an iconic symbol of early 20th-century modernism.

It has been revealed that it’s also a symbol of Nazi persecution. In 1932, the school closed under pressure from state Nazi officials that denounced the Bauhaus as un-German, internationalist, and a hotbed of “cultural Bolshevism.” (It briefly operated in Berlin, until it fell to Nazi pressure there, too.) Many of its members fled the Nazi regime and are now considered some of the last century’s most influential luminaries of art, architecture, and design.

Nazis burn anti-German literature in Berlin on May 11, 1933.

Recent findings suggest that clear, simple, and functional, Bauhaus’s influence has been a key German cultural export for more than a century. Yet Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a culture policy spokesman for the AfD, considers it an “Irrweg der Moderne”—“a wrong turn of modernity.” For years, he has targeted the Bauhaus, arguing that it stands for “deracination” and “dislocation of architecture” in favor of a “globalist” architectural vernacular. The Bauhaus was not only an aesthetic movement, he suggests, but a deeply political—and dangerously anti-German—project that must be combatted for the sake of German identity today.

In September, the AfD swept the state elections of Saxony Anhalt, where Dessau is located, which means that Tillschneider—who’s been a member of Saxony Anhalt’s parliament for a decade—may soon be in a position to realize his ambitions for recasting German culture. And those ambitions extend far beyond the Bauhaus.

The AfD’s electoral victory put it within reach of forming Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II, with the power to determine educational and cultural policies for the region. Right now, its 39 seats in the 83-member parliament leave it three votes short of an absolute majority (although other parties have ruled out a formal coalition). The party is hoping its candidate for state premier, Ulrich Siegmund, will be officially confirmed by the state legislature in early December.

It has been revealed that if the AfD successfully forms a government, there may be significant cuts to funding for a host of cultural institutions in the state, including the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, which operates in the school’s original building (which is now mostly converted into a museum). The AfD has not only positioned itself as the hardline party on immigration, but more broadly as a party seeking to culturally reform Germany. And, for the AfD, broad swathes of what has long been recognized as German culture are simply “un-German.”.

Sources indicate that for a party rooted in the former East, much of the offending inheritance belongs to the postwar West. Germany’s self-image as an internationalist, socially liberal state and leader by example in reckoning with its Nazi past have defined reunified Germany. The AfD, by contrast, wants to treat Nazi Germany as a historical aberration. In this sense, the AfD’s cultural policies are not only restorative of neglected aspects of German history, as it likes to claim, but a revisionist effort to redefine substantial parts of the country’s recent past.

According to recent reports, asked in an email which major German cultural figures belonged in the national canon, Tillschneider had a ready taxonomy. Thomas Mann, the Nobel laureate who became a prominent opponent of Hitler from exile, yes. But Günter Grass and Heinrich Böll, both Nobel-winning novelists whose work helped shape West Germany’s critical examination of its past and present, would be forgotten along with “the whole postwar lot.”.

German author Thomas Mann at his home in New York City in January 1943.Fred Stein Archive/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that he similarly dismissed much of the work of Rainer Werner Fassbinder—a leading figure in New German Cinema whose films examined the cruelties and compromises beneath postwar prosperity—as bound to its time. Leni Riefenstahl, the filmmaker who notoriously made propaganda films for the Nazi regime, received a more favorable assessment. The continuing interest in her work outside official channels, he argued, suggested that the filmmaker’s innovations would endure.

In a recent development, for Tillschneider, the distinction was not simply between artists who had opposed Nazism and those who had accommodated or served it. It concerned what their work could offer Germans now. “We don’t want to ban it,” he noted of art he considered anti-German. “But art that turns against Germany cannot claim a right to continued support from the German taxpayer.”.

Tillschneider’s hostility to modernism is not confined to Dessau. Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie, designed by the Bauhaus’s last director, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and opened in West Berlin in 1968, is “a hideous lump,” he noted. The government quarter inspired a more physical response: “I regularly feel like throwing up when I walk behind the Reichstag and see those bland cubes of steel, glass, and concrete,” he wrote.

Sources indicate that the Neue Nationalgalerie, a museum of 20th-century art, in Berlin on Aug. 29, 1969. Hedrich Blessing Collection/Getty Images.

While these judgments represent the personal preferences of one far-right politician, they may also soon determine how government money is spent. This is of outsized importance in Germany, where cultural infrastructure is in large part sustained by public funding.

Sources indicate that since the September state election, the AfD has already sought substantial cuts to theater funding. In October, its city council faction proposed prepares to reduce Theatre Magdeburg’s annual municipal subsidy by up to 7 million euros.

While the party presented the proposal as a response to the city’s financial difficulties, in the months preceding the election, the theater’s general director, Julien Chavaz, publicly rejected the idea that theater should enact a conservative program and warned that to attack theater is itself “anti-German.” The city council rejected the AfD’s motion in November, signaling the resistance the AfD’s cultural policies still face.

In a recent development, tillschneider’s arguments echo a broader AfD campaign against the place of national self-criticism in German public life. In a speech in 2017, the AfD’s hard-right ideological standard-bearer, Björn Höcke, demanded a “180-degree turn in our policy of memory.” He called the monument to murdered Jews in Berlin a “monument of shame,” and attacked the framing of Germany’s defeat in World War II as liberation from Nazism.

In a recent development, read More A supporter of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds up a placard that indicates AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund just before initial results indicated the party with 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt state elections, in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sept. 6. A supporter of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds up a placard that shows AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund just before initial results showed the party with 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt state elections, in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sept. 6. Why AfD Appeals to So Many Germans The far-right party surges in a regional election. Insider | Cameron Abadi, Adam Tooze.

The far-right party surges in a regional election.

In 2023, AfD cultural spokesman Marc Jongen argued in the federal legislature that Germany increasingly reduced being German to “an exclusively negative self-image” and his faction proposed reorienting cultural policy toward “positive” sources of national identity. Tillschneider gives that ambition specific cultural targets, identifying the writers, institutions, and forms of remembrance he believes should lose public support or prominence: “We must finally arrive at an identity unburdened by the Nazi era,” he wrote.

And Tillschneider—who could have a say in setting cultural and educational policy in any AfD-led government in Saxony-Anhalt—is happy to provide reading lists to achieve that goal. In our email exchange, he called for state assistance for contemporary writers such as Jörg Bernig and Uwe Tellkamp. Bernig, an award-winning poet and novelist, and Tellkamp, whose novel The Tower won the German Book Prize, have become controversial for their criticism of immigration policy and allegations that German cultural life marginalizes conservative views.

He recommended renewed attention to Martin Heidegger, the influential philosopher who joined the Nazi Party and whose writings contain antisemitic passages, and praised projects that adapted German poetry and folk songs for contemporary audiences.

In a recent development, tillschneider also gave Ernst Jünger, the author of the World War I memoir Storm of Steel and a leading voice of radical nationalism during the Weimar Republic, a stronger claim to the canon than either Grass or Böll, saying his work should be read in schools and he should be publicly commemorated. (Jünger himself refused to join the Nazi Party.).

German author Ernst Jünger at his home in Wilflingen, Germany, in February 1974.Sven Simon Archives/Getty Images.

His recommendations were notably not exclusively literary; he praised a version of Goethe’s “Heidenröslein” set to a techno beat.

It has been revealed that asked whether the postwar tradition of national self-criticism was itself part of German culture, Tillschneider acknowledged that it was. But its German origins did not establish its value. “This tradition of self-criticism is, of course, German,” he wrote. “The question is whether it ought to belong to Germany, whether we can make use of it to sustain our identity.”.

That position helps explain his dismissal of much of Germany’s postwar cultural inheritance. The capacity to question Germany, including the incongruities between its democratic present and its authoritarian past, has itself traditionally been understood as a national achievement of modern German culture. What Tillschneider considers exhausted or destructive in Germany’s culture of self-examination could equally be understood as one of postwar Germany’s enduring cultural accomplishments.

As for National Socialism, Tillschneider noted it should continue to be studied in schools, universities, memorial sites, and among research institutions. But it should become a historical subject, rather than a tool for interpreting the present or future. The reality of National Socialism, he argued, should leave older German traditions untainted by association.

According to recent reports, tillschneider treats his own tastes as expressions of national identity, while treating art that challenges that identity as political. He’s quick to describe his aesthetic preferences as a neutral standard; departures from them become ideology. In our email exchange, he called for public funding to support predominantly “pure,” apolitical art. But greater attention to nationalist writers, or to art organized around German identity, did not strike him as a departure from that principle. “National identity is not a political subject,” he wrote.

For Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, the AfD’s political accusations against the Bauhaus today, like those of the Nazis 100 years before, are fundamentally mistaken. She emphasized that, for all its modernist ambitions, the Bauhaus had never been politically uniform, much less stridently anti-German.

During a visit to the museum in early October, I struggled to find the radicalism that so offends the AfD. The exhibitions I saw foregrounded materials and production, giving an institution that had sought to transform everyday life a surprisingly subdued presentation. The Bauhaus, however, remains indelibly political to Tillschneider. It should, he argued, have developed traditional building practices to meet upcoming human needs instead of seeking a rupture with the past.

In a recent development, but according to Steiner, the Bauhaus Museum and foundation is an authentic expression of 20th-century German history. “I would say the Bauhaus is German and not German at the same time. It’s both,” Steiner stated. “Without the Weimar Republic, there would have been no Bauhaus. Without [East Germany], it would not have been reopened.”.

According to recent reports, moreover, Steiner insists, the movement is deeply rooted in German tradition at the local, national, and international level. “The Bauhaus had—and still has—a great many connections to Dessau, to the region, but also to the world,” she said. “I cannot separate them.”.

Carol Schaeffer is a writer and journalist based in Berlin.

Tech Report: Why deep pockets weren’t enough to save the GOP in 2026: 'Money is not magic'

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.
  • Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.
  • Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.

Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.

Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.

The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night.

MUSK PICKS HIS FIRST GOP WARRIORS AS A 2026 MONEY SURGE TAKES SHAPE.

GOP electoral efforts were buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC. (Getty Images).

On top of their already significant nine-figure lead, GOP electoral efforts were also buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC — which themselves collected an additional $665.4 million for Republicans to burn through. Despite such a massive financial edge, the GOP suffered one of its worst midterm performances in history, losing Senate seats even in deep red jurisdictions like South Carolina and Mississippi.

Still, Capital Research Center President Scott Walter, argues: "Money is not magic.".

"Democrats should remember that when tempted to curtail political speech with donation limits, and Republicans should remember that when tempted to think more money automatically means more votes," the leader of the right-of-center group told Fox News Digital. "That will be news to those like Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., who thinks billionaires and ‘dark money’ control the cosmos.".

Walter pointed out, citing data aggregated by OpenSecrets, that the biggest donor in any given election cycle rarely ends up getting what they want out of the American political system.

Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets, a nonprofit dedicated to tracking money in politics, told Fox News Digital that, while money certainly moves the needle in elections, its actual impact can be blunted by a variety of factors — many of which were at play during the recent midterms.

AI IS SUPERCHARGING POLITICAL AD WARS. BUT VIRAL DOESN’T MEAN VICTORIOUS.

Elon Musk presents a $1 million check during an America PAC town hall ahead of the Wisconsin Supreme Court election, in Green Bay, Wisconsin, on March 30, 2025. (Jamie Kelter Davis/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

"​​Certainly, you know, the money makes a difference," said Glavin.

Sources indicate that "When both sides are engaging in a sort of arms race, right, and they're both spending almost equivalently, then really the effect is lost," he explained. "If you're somebody [who] sees an ad for one candidate, and then it's immediately followed by an ad for another candidate… essentially, you're not moving the needle.".

In many of the marquee races of Election Day, such as the Senate races in Texas and Michigan, both parties had enough money to saturate the airwaves with their messaging, potentially creating the environment described by Glavin.

According to recent reports, "This election was very unique," he told Fox News Digital. "What people probably really didn’t see until afterward is there was this significant headwind and voters were feeling a certain way and more ads were not going to change that.".

SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL.

According to recent reports, "I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the massive SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," one expert stated. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

Glavin, to support his argument, pointed to the fact that self-funding candidates running in elections often fail to make much headway, serving as evidence for the claim that ludicrous amounts of money don’t automatically equate to political success.

One of the most obvious recent examples is former Fresh York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who spent roughly $1.1 billion of his own money on his 2020 presidential campaign. He won only 55 delegates in the Democratic primaries at an approximate cost of $18 million per delegate.

Academics who spoke to Fox News Digital were divided on the impact money has on elections.

Recent findings suggest that "Money has diminishing returns," Ray La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told Fox News Digital. "And in [an] election wave environment where the president and his party is overwhelmingly disliked or distrusted, money can do little to save them.".

JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026.

Industry observers note that michael Bloomberg discusses his presidential run on Nov. 25, 2019, in Norfolk, Virginia. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images).

John Sides, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University, meanwhile, pointed Fox News Digital to a 2022 study he and two other academics conducted studying the impact of television advertising on election outcomes.

According to their study, there is a relatively direct relationship between ad spending and voter share and, while there is a degree of diminishing returns in elections with very high spending, there is still a marginal impact.

Joe Arlinghaus, a Texas-based conservative political strategist, told Fox News Digital that how money is spent matters more than how much of it is spent, an assertion he mentioned could explain why the GOP did so poorly despite its hefty cash advantage.

Industry observers note that "Most people understand that new technologies get better and better and better as time goes on," he remarked. "Bugs get worked out. Inferior practitioners get pushed aside. Trial and error leads to better and better practices. This is what has been happening in the Democratic election world.".

He noted that Republicans have failed to keep up on that front.

"I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the significant SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," Arlinghaus added.

Glavin shared that perspective, noting how "Musk just recently commented about how he may be regretting a little bit all the money he spent.".

"It's hard to tell how serious he is about that and whether or not he'll just come back again for the next election," he added, speculating that the massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving.

THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES.

According to recent reports, democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin addresses party members at the DNC's summer meeting, on Aug. 25, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Paul Steinhauser - Fox News).

One source familiar with Republican politics told Fox News Digital that "advertisements pay for mortgages in Great Falls," a reference to claims that political consultants spend money in ways that make them wealthier, not necessarily in ways that help candidates win. Great Falls is a wealthy suburb of Washington, D.C.

Recent findings suggest that while Republicans enjoyed an overall fundraising advantage, largely driven by wealthy large-dollar donors, individual Democratic candidates in high-priority races generally raised more money than their Republican rivals, as was the case in Georgia, Michigan and Texas’s Senate elections, among other contests. Some say this should have been an early warning sign for the GOP that grassroots support was wavering, though others are skeptical of such an assertion.

Colin Seeberger, the chief strategy officer at the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal advocacy group, told Fox News Digital that the fundraising advantages enjoyed by individual Democrats were a "reflection of voters' enthusiasm for those individual campaigns.".

He also said voters had an "overwhelming frustration with the direction of the country and how the president and majorities in Congress … were disconnected from what voters said that they wanted [from] the people of their government.".

BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS.

It has been revealed that the massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving, one expert noted. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images).

"I'm not sure that the party that raises more definitively has an enthusiasm advantage," Sides, the Vanderbilt professor, remarked, pointing to past elections where Democrats have secured more donations than the GOP but lost anyway.

Seeberger echoed Arlinghaus’ claim that Republicans may have squandered some of their financial advantage by making poor spending decisions, saying, "When you're spending the majority of those sums to talk about issues that register low on the rankings of what voters say are their priorities, there's going to be limited returns on the impact.".

#122541. The Real Nvidia Scandal

The Real Nvidia Scandal

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emily Kilcrease is Senior Fellow and Director of the Energy, Economics, and Security Program at the Center for a Fresh American Security.
  • Vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Latest American Security.
  • How China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emily Kilcrease is Senior Fellow and Director of the Energy, Economics, and Security Program at the Center for a Fresh American Security. From 2019 to 2021, first in the Trump administration and then in the Biden administration, she was Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Investment.

Vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Latest American Security. He previously served as Legislative Director to Senator Michael Bennet and as a policy adviser at the U.S. Department of State.

How China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S. National Security—and How Congress Can Close It.

Emily Kilcrease and Vivek Chilukuri.

The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia this week added another twist to a scandal that has transfixed Washington and Silicon Valley. The stakes go beyond the swings of the stock market or the salacious details about Huang’s affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed and a potential Chinese asset. At its core, the scandal has exposed something that matters far more than any one man or manufacturer: American export-control policy remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy. Unless Washington fixes this, it risks imperiling the United States’ hard-won advantage in artificial intelligence.

Industry observers note that this export policy failure is more than the sum of specific deficiencies. It stems from the Trump administration’s broader posture on China. Washington has embraced unfettered AI acceleration at the same time as it has struck a more accommodating stance toward Beijing. That combination set the stage for the explosive Megaspeed scandal—and perhaps others that have yet to emerge. As a result, China has been able to access an alarming number of advanced chips that have enabled it to narrow the AI gap with the United States and power its AI-driven military modernization. According to the AI research institute Epoch AI, up to a third of China’s AI computing power may come from smuggled chips. China’s top AI models are now just months behind the U.S. frontier. The narrow gap reflects China’s genuine innovation and access to abundant energy resources as well as its relentless efforts to circumvent U.S. controls.

It has been revealed that huang’s return to Nvidia at the behest of President Donald Trump suggests that both the manufacturer and the White House seem utterly uninterested in keeping powerful AI chips from China. It will instead fall to Congress to ensure that the United States leverages its compute advantage and maintains its AI edge. The midterm elections and mounting bipartisan concerns over the Megaspeed debacle give Congress upcoming momentum to correct course. Its near-term agenda should include closing known loopholes that played a key role in allowing Megaspeed to supply advanced chips to China, stepping up enforcement of existing controls, and strengthening oversight of the administration’s export-control decisions.

According to recent reports, over the medium term, Congress must also tackle the broader question of how to balance the strategic benefits of exporting U.S. technology to build the world’s AI infrastructure with robust controls to prevent its leakage to China. The long-standing debate over which American AI chips and capabilities Washington should permit to diffuse globally and under what conditions has finally boiled over into the mainstream—and, in a perverse way, the national security community can thank Alice Huang for forcing the issue.

The issue before Congress, however, is much broader than addressing the specifics of the Nvidia scandal. Congress must also contend with the underlying impulses driving the administration’s China policy and install guardrails to avoid the erosion of U.S. export controls. This means that after Congress passes near-term bills to mop up the Megaspeed mess, it must then take the reins on setting long-term export-control strategy.

Recent findings suggest that congress cannot stand by idly as AI blazes forward. OpenAI’s top model can now perform professional tasks as well as or better than humans 85 percent of the time, up from just 14 percent in 2024. The time an AI model can independently work on a task is doubling every four months. Last week, a researcher at Anthropic unveiled that AI helped him untangle the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous problems in pure mathematics.

As capabilities have grown, so have risks. Frontier models can now complete simulated cyberattacks on networks on their own, and hackers are using AI models to partially automate their attacks. In the July incident involving the AI platform Hugging Face, rogue AI agents escaped their testing environment and plotted to evade human oversight, underscoring the difficulty of aligning model behavior with human intent. The growing power of AI and the risks from misuse or loss of control make U.S. leadership a national security imperative.

According to recent reports, at its core, the U.S.-Chinese AI competition boils down to which country can deploy the best chips in the highest quantities to train and adopt advanced AI models. The Biden administration’s controls slowed Chinese AI developers by leaving them with fewer, worse chips. Nvidia’s top Blackwell chips are nearly seven times better than Huawei’s Ascend equivalents. By the end of 2026, Huawei will likely have produced less than four percent of the compute that Nvidia will have over the same time. As the founder and CEO of DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI companies, admitted in 2024, “Our problem has never been money—it’s the embargo on high-end chips.”.

To circumvent Biden-era restrictions, elaborate networks for smuggling and transshipment emerged to divert chips to China from other countries that could legally acquire them, and Chinese companies leveraged export-control loopholes to remotely access U.S.-powered compute through data centers abroad. Chinese firms funded companies such as Megaspeed to facilitate these workarounds. Backed by the Chinese tech giant Alibaba, Megaspeed has purchased $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips since 2023, prompting an investigation from the U.S. government. Chinese companies also used a technique known as adversarial distillation—training their models on the outputs of top U.S. models at a fraction of the compute. All of this needlessly shrank the United States’ AI lead over China, even after the imposition of export controls.

Recent findings suggest that these developments should have spurred the Trump administration to better resource, enforce, and revision the export controls when it came into office. It did the opposite. In May 2025, the administration suspended the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule, which had established rules for which countries could access advanced chips and in what quantities. Then, after initially prohibiting sales to China of Nvidia’s H20 chip, which was custom-built as a less powerful product for the Chinese market, the Trump administration reversed course in December 2025 and greenlighted the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chip. Although the H200 is two generations behind top U.S. chips, it remains superior to anything China can produce. An investigation from the House Foreign Affairs Committee in November revealed that between December 2025 and May 2026, the Trump administration approved the sale of more than 800,000 of Nvidia’s H200 chips and AMD’s MI325X equivalent, including to companies that the Pentagon has designated as linked to the Chinese military. This week, under pressure from Congress, the administration added Megaspeed to the entity list, which blocks those listed from buying U.S. products without a license—but before that, the administration had not added a single new individual or business to the list in 2026.

Sources indicate that this regulatory vacuum and policy incoherence created the perfect conditions for Megaspeed. The Singaporean firm at the center of the Nvidia scandal seems tailor-made to operate in the seams of U.S. export controls. In 2024, the Commerce Department initiated a formal investigation of the company, which could have led to sanctions such as being placed on the entity list. But the Trump administration dragged its feet in pursuing the investigation. In the meantime, Megaspeed stocked Southeast Asian data centers with thousands of U.S. chips, enabling remote access for Chinese firms. This remote access loophole in U.S. export controls was a well-known and increasingly popular workaround for China-linked firms, but the Trump administration left it open for nearly two years and closed it only last week amid pressure from the Nvidia scandal. Regardless of the Megaspeed specifics, the net result of the Trump administration’s actions and inaction is that China has enjoyed access to far more computing power than it should have during a vital period of the AI competition.

It has been revealed that the administration’s long-awaited closure of the remote access loophole is a welcome step. The rule requires foreign data centers to secure a license before offering significant computing power to China-based customers. It also requires a license to export advanced chips to places that could facilitate remote access and chip diversion, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. This rule will make it harder for firms such as Megaspeed to import chips in the first place, or to use them to serve China-based customers. But the rule will be difficult to enforce because the U.S. Commerce Department does not have the legal authority under export controls to directly regulate services such as cloud computing. More key, the administration’s lax enforcement of past controls—and internal divisions over the latest ones—raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through. Huang’s reinstatement as CEO, with Trump’s backing, will make it harder to vigorously enforce these new controls and move toward a tougher posture on China.

In a recent development, since Congress cannot rely on the administration to fix export controls and protect the United States’ AI lead, lawmakers should urgently advance bipartisan measures to address the underlying conditions that gave rise to entities such as Megaspeed. As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an crucial first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track “on-chip” technologies—basically, features that can verify a chip’s location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world’s legacy chips.

Along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. Congress can go even further by establishing a new investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive.

It has been revealed that at the same time, closing loopholes and codifying rules is insufficient to fix the underlying issues that led to the Megaspeed scandal in the first place. This mess is directly downstream from Trump’s dovish shift on China that has seen the administration take a softer line on Beijing just as the AI race accelerated. The administration’s own overreach forced Washington into a conciliatory posture. Administration officials failed to realize that China had learned its lesson from the first Trump administration’s trade wars and was poised to retaliate hard in the second term. After China responded to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and export controls with its own punishing controls on rare earths, the Trump administration found its way into a vaguely defined and fragile truce. This has severely constrained U.S. policymaking, including related to compute controls.

According to recent reports, indeed, Trump became an easy sell for advocates of aggressive AI promotion such as Jensen Huang. This camp argues that U.S. leadership in the global AI race requires pushing American AI technologies to as many parts of the globe as possible—including China. They claim that keeping China “addicted” to the U.S. AI stack gives Washington leverage and outweighs the national security concerns that could come with helping China improve its AI capabilities. Huang even pushed demonstrably false narratives that China’s military was not interested in Nvidia’s chips and labeled his critics as “unpatriotic” for not wanting U.S. chips spread as far and wide as possible and therefore depriving American tech firms of global market share.

Trump, who was interested in stabilizing the relationship with China and prioritizing near-term, transactional victories on trade, bought it. He also broke with decades of U.S. foreign policy precedent to negotiate export controls with China. In a series of “do nothing” leader-level meetings since, the president has emphasized summitry optics over pushing China on any sensitive challenges. And Huang’s restoration at Nvidia ensures that the president’s worst impulses on China will continue to be egged on by his favored tech CEO, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

In a recent development, A core part of Congress’s longer-term agenda should be outlining the basic principles to determine who can import or remotely access advanced AI chips and under what conditions. Administrations have gone back and forth over this line-drawing exercise. The Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule would have imposed a global licensing regime that controlled not just the export of chips but also the aggregate U.S.-powered compute that any country could receive. Under Trump, only a handful of countries face restrictions. A smarter approach would condition advanced chip sales on the buyer’s ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules. Allied and partner governments could demonstrate this by developing robust economic security policies to prevent chip diversion or remote access. Foreign companies would have to show strong compliance and security commitments. In practice, this would mean having internal procedures to ensure that chips are not diverted and maintaining cooperation with Commerce Department officials to verify that such procedures were working.

According to recent reports, congress can also help rebuild allies’ confidence in U.S. export-control policy. There was hard-won, if imperfect, progress on allied alignment in key areas of export controls under the Biden administration, notably with the Dutch and the Japanese on controls of semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The painstaking work needed to get allies on board can be agonizingly slow, but once achieved, it is far more likely to endure than if the United States imposes extraterritorial controls over their objections. The MATCH Act, one of the bills revived following the Megaspeed scandal, requires controls on allied-produced tools if Washington is unable to negotiate allied alignment. It is a rather rude approach at a moment when U.S. export controls seem to be on shaky footing, U.S. tariffs against allies have pushed relations to a near breaking point, and allies rightly question whether the United States still views China as a strategic threat. Instead, Congress should support efforts to create durable frameworks for allied alignment, such as economic security agreements in key strategic sectors.

Recent findings suggest that A longer-term agenda must include fixing the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, the main agency responsible for administering and enforcing export controls. The bureau has been gutted by dismissals and low morale during the Trump administration, but it has been underresourced for far longer. Congress should increase funding and require modernization of the bureau’s antiquated IT system. Just as notable, Congress needs to help insulate policymaking decisions from corporate influence, and it can help by insisting that future Commerce Department officials commit to independent and risk-based decision-making to earn confirmation.

Industry observers note that none of these steps will be easy. The president’s support of Huang’s restoration indicates that stock market fluctuations weigh more heavily in his decision-making than national security, and the administration is unlikely to welcome increased congressional oversight. The Constitution gives the executive wide deference on matters of foreign policy and national security. But Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States’ AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at fresh proposed U.S. tariffs on China and other trade partners, tensions between Ukraine and Libya over a drone attack, and the end of a long deportation battle in the United States.

World Brief will be off Thursday and Friday for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. We will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a fresh batch of tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, including China, Japan, South Korea, and the European Union.

The proposed tariff rates, which could be implemented early next year, range from 15 percent for the EU, Taiwan, and South Korea, 18 percent for most others, and rates of as much as 25 percent on India or 35 percent on Vietnam. China faces a fresh tariff rate of 20 percent, which will be stacked on top of duties still lingering from U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term—and that’s only if the trade truce between Beijing and Washington holds. (It expires in January.).

It has been revealed that the latest tariffs are the culmination of an investigation launched this spring into alleged excess industrial capacity among nearly all U.S. trading partners. U.S. trade officials allege that other countries artificially prop up their manufacturing sectors with subsidies, promotions, tax breaks, and other measures that distort trade and disadvantage U.S. exports. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has taken equity stakes in dozens of private companies and is actively promoting state involvement in the manufacture of everything from chips to ships.

China’s Foreign Ministry said the new tariffs are based on a “false proposition,” though China is one of the few countries among the 14 economies targeted that demonstrates genuine excess capacity that is harming the U.S. and global economies. Even trade specialists who are skeptical of the Trump administration’s affinity for tariffs believe that higher duties on Chinese exports are warranted.

The European Commission also hit back at the tariffs, arguing that Europe is a victim of overcapacity, not a source of the problem.

Sources indicate that the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act to levy the upcoming duties—the same law that it used earlier this year to slap tariffs on 60 economies on the grounds that they do not adequately police forced labor in their supply chains. (Those tariffs were challenged in court.) The proposed new tariffs would essentially replace (and slightly raise) the rates levied earlier, implying that the question of forced labor has been solved in just a few months.

Sources indicate that the measures proposed on Wednesday are just the latest attempt by the Trump administration to find a formula to recreate in the aggregate the sweeping global tariffs that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down earlier this year. The administration has used at least four different trade authorities dating back almost a century to continue raising barriers to trade, despite polls showing that the widespread unpopularity of tariffs contributed to the Republicans’ historic midterm election wipeout.

According to recent reports, toxic explosives. The U.S. Army on Wednesday blew up nearly five tons of toxic lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. The intentional detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide, a sensitive chemical compound used by the military in explosives, was originally scheduled to take place last Friday. The controlled explosion was delayed, however, amid public pushback and legal challenges from environmental groups.

Destroying the bomb-making material, which had been stored in the Iowa plant since 2009, was deemed necessary by the military after inspectors in March discovered that it had partially crystallized—increasing the risk of a spontaneous explosion. But the plan to detonate the material raised concerns over the potential for toxic lead dust to spread over a large area, and many locals also said they weren’t given enough notice to prepare.

Residents within five miles of the blast were urged to evacuate ahead of the detonation, while others in the vicinity were told to remain indoors.

After the detonation, the Environmental Protection Agency wrote on X that its real-time air monitors were reporting “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region.” Adam Telle, the Army’s acting secretary, also wrote on X that the “controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success” and mentioned the threat of an “uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated.”.

Recent findings suggest that ukraine and Libya. Kyiv has seemingly angered the primary military force in eastern Libya, the Libyan National Army (LNA), after attacking a Russian warship that was refueling at the Benghazi Naval Base on Sunday. Two Libyan naval officers died from wounds sustained in the Ukrainian sea drone attack. The LNA has vowed to retaliate “at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means.”.

Ukraine offered no immediate public response on Wednesday, though officials said the previous day that Ukrainian forces hadn’t targeted Libyans in the operation.

Recent findings suggest that the incident is yet another example of how the Russia-Ukraine war has spread to other parts of the globe. Russian missiles crashed in Poland last week, and there have been repeated Russian drone incursions on NATO’s eastern flank. Ukraine also carried out a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland this past weekend.

A ‘free man.’ Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrived in Spain on Wednesday as part of a negotiated agreement between the Salvadoran immigrant’s attorneys and the U.S. government after a prolonged, highly publicized deportation battle with the Trump administration. “I’m happy, and I’m celebrating my freedom,” Abrego Garcia told reporters in Spanish after he landed.

It has been revealed that amid the administration’s controversial crackdown on immigration, Abrego Garcia was arrested last year by federal agents in Maryland, wrongfully deported, and placed in a notorious prison in El Salvador before he was ultimately brought back to the United States. The Trump administration continued to target Abrego Garcia for deportation and aimed to send him to Liberia, but that was blocked by the courts.

Recent findings suggest that simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, noted that his client left the United States a “free man” and signaled that Abrego Garcia would attempt to return once Trump is no longer in office. “Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to outlast Donald Trump, and he’ll be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident,” he said.

Sources indicate that on Wednesday, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first Pakistani national to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station. Ali, who will return to Earth in a few days, told reporters that he carries “the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.” We officially feel like underachievers.

Latest Update: The Paradox of Iranian Power

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs
